subject: English
summaryPoints: Connectors of addition (and, also, besides, furthermore, moreover, in addition) link supporting ideas, whereas sequence connectors (first, next, then, meanwhile, eventually, finally) establish chronological cohesion.
Adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, seldom, never) specify habitual frequency; they precede main verbs but follow copular 'be' and auxiliary/modal verbs.
Simple past tense denotes events completed at a definite time in the past using regular (-d/-ed) and irregular verb changes.
Past continuous denotes an ongoing past activity, frequently forming interrupted action sentences when combined with simple past using 'when' and 'while'.
Compound sentences connect two independent clauses via coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or), while complex sentences combine an independent clause with one or more dependent clauses.
Collocations form natural combinations: adjective + noun ('heavy traffic', 'rich culture', 'strong wind') and verb + preposition ('break down', 'boil down to', 'blow up').

formulas.label: Interrupted Past Action Formula
formulas.expr: While + S + was/were + V-ing, S + V2(past simple)  OR  S + was/were + V-ing + when + S + V2(past simple)

formulas.label: Adverb of Frequency Word Order
formulas.expr: S + Adverb of Frequency + Main Verb  OR  S + be/modal + Adverb of Frequency

formulas.label: Compound Sentence Structure
formulas.expr: Independent Clause + , + Coordinating Conjunction (and, but, or) + Independent Clause

formulas.label: Complex Sentence Structure
formulas.expr: Subordinating Conjunction + Dependent Clause + , + Independent Clause  OR  Independent Clause + Subordinating Conjunction + Dependent Clause

examTip: In EUEE sentence combination items, pay close attention to conjunction choices: 'While' is followed by the continuous aspect ('While she was driving...'), whereas 'When' commonly introduces the simple past punctive event that interrupts it ('...when the tire burst').

keyDefinitions.definition: A habitual and predictable pairing or grouping of two or more words that naturally co-occur in standard English usage.
A transitional word or phrase (e.g., moreover, furthermore, in addition) used to introduce supplementary corroborating information.
A transitional cohesive device (e.g., first, subsequently, meanwhile, finally) that orders actions or events chronologically.
A sentence composed of two or more coordinate independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction or semicolon.

eueeFocusTopics: Conjunctions of addition vs contrast (furthermore vs however)
Past continuous and past simple clause blending with 'when' and 'while'
Syntactic position of frequency adverbs relative to auxiliary and main verbs
Fixed adjective-noun collocations (heavy rain, strong smell, big mistake)
Phrasal verbs based on 'blow' and 'break' (break down, break out, blow up)
